raw.answer: Fifty-one legislators challenged amendments to the Constitutional Court Procedure Act passed in December 2024 and promulgated in January 2025. The amendments required at least 10 justices to deliberate and 9 to strike down a law, among other changes. The court found the amendments unconstitutional because of a seriously flawed legislative process and because they violate separation of powers, so they lose effect.
raw.held: The court declared the challenged provisions (Art. 4(3), Art. 30(2)-(6) and Art. 95) unconstitutional, and they lose effect on the day the judgment is announced. The pre-amendment Art. 95 continues to apply, and the request for a provisional order was dismissed.

points.text: The court would not apply the challenged 10-justice threshold to judge itself, since a rule under review cannot also be the procedure used to review it. It used the earlier rule based on two-thirds of the current total for deliberation and a majority for decision, and did not count three justices who persistently refused to take part.
The petition was admitted because the 51 legislators exceeded the one-quarter threshold, and the record shows they did not support the bills in the final votes.

The legislative process had obvious, serious defects. Contents entirely different from the original proposal were introduced during clause-by-clause discussion, there was almost no real debate, and the third reading was never put to a vote, which breached the principles of openness and discussion.
Article 4(3) required the President to nominate within two months, which imposes a duty the Constitution does not provide and so breaches separation of powers.

The fixed minimum of 10 justices, with no safeguard for vacancies, could repeatedly halt the Court because the President and Legislative Yuan control appointments. Paragraphs 3 and 4 depend on it and fall with it.
Paragraphs 5 and 6 apply to almost only one situation and set inconsistent thresholds. Art. 95 muddled the effective dates of earlier versions of the Act, causing legal uncertainty.

who: The President and the Legislative Yuan
